title: Dynamical and conformational behavior of a polymer in a crowded solution
abstract: We investigate the structure and dynamics of a polymer in a fluid containing mobile spherical colloidal crowders of radius $R$. We compare and contrast the behavior with Langevin dynamics (LD) and lattice--Boltzmann molecular dynamics (LBMD), the latter incorporating long-range hydrodynamic interactions. Both the colloid size relative to the monomer radius $r$ and the volume fraction $φ$ are varied to determine how crowding modifies polymer behavior. Increasing volume fraction induces polymer compaction, with the mechanism strongly dependent on the size ratio $R/r$. Small colloids primarily modify the short-wavelength polymer conformation, causing self-avoiding-walk-like behavior to persist to shorter length scales, whereas large colloids reduce the effective long-wavelength Flory exponent, indicating degraded solvent quality consistent with a confinement-blob picture. Polymer diffusion exhibits distinct behavior in LD and LBMD. In LD, diffusion decreases rapidly and depends strongly on $R/r$; a phenomenological scaling involving $\ln(1+R/r)$ captures this size dependence, and additional scaling with $R_g$ reduces scatter, indicating polymer-scale correlations induced by crowding. In contrast, LBMD diffusion follows an effective-medium-like exponential dependence on concentration, governed by hydrodynamic coupling. Rouse-mode analysis identifies three regimes: scaling breakdown at low volume fraction, Zimm-like behavior at intermediate density in both LD and LB, and at high density hydrodynamic screening in LB with confinement-dominated dynamics in LD.
summary: This work simulates a polymer in a crowded colloidal solution using both Langevin Dynamics and Lattice-Boltzmann Molecular Dynamics. It finds that crowding causes polymer compaction, and crucially, the inclusion of full hydrodynamic interactions (LBMD) yields different, more physically accurate scaling laws for diffusion compared to simpler models. This underscores the necessity of accurate solvent coupling in polymer physics simulations.
main_problem: The study investigates how the presence of mobile colloidal crowders modifies the static structure and dynamic behavior of a polymer chain in a fluid.
main_result: Crowding induces polymer compaction, with large colloids degrading the effective long-wavelength Flory exponent, while polymer diffusion exhibits distinct size-dependent scaling when comparing Langevin Dynamics (LD) to full hydrodynamic simulations (LBMD).
method: The authors employed molecular simulations, comparing Langevin Dynamics (LD) with Lattice-Boltzmann Molecular Dynamics (LBMD) to model polymer-colloid interactions.
model_or_system: The system consists of a polymer chain interacting with mobile spherical colloidal crowders in a fluid. The simulation models include FENE bonds, Lennard-Jones interactions, and the LBMD approach explicitly incorporates long-range hydrodynamic interactions.
key_observables: Polymer compaction, diffusion coefficient (D), radius of gyration ($R_g$), and Rouse-mode relaxation times ($	au_p$).
important_parameters: Colloid size ratio ($R/r$), volume fraction ($\phi$), and the comparison between LD and LBMD simulation frameworks.
main_assumptions: LD simulations assume an implicit solvent lacking long-range hydrodynamics, while LBMD explicitly couples particle motion to the fluid momentum exchange.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the system setup, polymer structure, and dynamic scaling behavior (e.g., $	au_p$ vs. $p/N$ for LD data, and exponent vs. $\phi$ for LB/Langevin simulations).
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the results from LD and LBMD simulations across varying colloid concentrations and sizes, analyzing structural changes (compaction, Flory exponent) and dynamic changes (diffusion, Rouse modes) to delineate the role of hydrodynamic interactions.
why_interesting: The detailed comparison between LD and LBMD highlights the critical importance of correctly modeling long-range hydrodynamic interactions in polymer dynamics, a concept relevant to open quantum systems where environmental coupling is crucial.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A schematic representation of the simulation system. (a) A polymer chain (yellow) is shown within the simulation box, sur- rounded by a crowded solution of mobile spherical colloids (red). (b) Each colloid consists of a central atom and a spherical surface shell. (c) Each monomer is similarly composed of a central atom and a smaller surface shell. Direct particle interactions, such as the FENE bond potential and Lennard-Jones repulsion, are applied between the central atoms, while the shell nodes interact with the Lattice- Boltzmann fluid to capture long-range hydrodynamic effects.

FIG. 2. a) The time autocorrelation of the end-to-end distance of the polymer as a function of lag time. The line corresponds to the fit of the time autocorrelation, which is used to determine the relaxation time of the polymer. b) Time evolution of Mean Squared Displace- ment (MSD), ⟨(r(t)−r(t′))2⟩in the absence of colloidal particles within the system. The lines correspond to the fits used to determine the diffusion constant D.

FIG. 3. The polymer radius of gyration normalized by its value in free solution, Rg/Rg0, as a function of the colloid volume fraction φ. Solid lines show the N = 96 lattice-Boltzmann results, dotted lines show the N = 96 Langevin-dynamics results, and dashed lines show the N = 192 Langevin-dynamics results.

FIG. 4. The polymer and colloid conformations in lattice Boltzmann simulations at low volume fraction of 0.10 for a) R=4nm, b) R=12nm, c) R=18nm, at intermediate volume fraction of 0.35 for d) R=4nm, e) R=12nm, f) R=18nm, and at high volume fraction of 0.60 for g) R=4nm, h) R=12nm, and i) R=18nm. Monomer clumps, or clusters, that will potentially give rise to de Gennes "blob"-like polymer behavior are indicated by the blue dashed regions. (Multimedia available online for (f) and (i))
